summary:
The legal framework a trans visitor meets in Meta Department stands under Colombia's national framework. Consensual same-sex activity has been legal since 1981, the Constitutional Court legalised same-sex marriage in April 2016, same-sex couples have held full adoption rights since 2015, and a 2011 law bans discrimination based on sexual orientation. Legal gender recognition has been available since 1993 on the basis of self-recognition, and since a rule change approved in June 2015 trans Colombians change the sex marker on government identification by signing a document before a notary, replacing the earlier route in which judges ordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025, and a comprehensive trans law remained under legislative consideration in 2025.

No source in the record reports any Meta-specific legal provision, enforcement practice or incident involving trans people. The assessment for the department therefore rests on the national pattern, which the sources describe as severe and worsening.

The gap between the written framework and enforcement is documented at national level. The Attorney General's Office recorded 35 LGBTI murders in Colombia between January and May 2025, and one report counted 13 trans people killed in the first quarter of 2025. The UN Independent Expert on sexual orientation and gender identity, Graeme Reid, completed a fact-finding mission across several Colombian cities in May 2025, praising the government's legal reforms and commitment to equality while warning that institutional progress and daily lived experience are disconnected and that widespread discrimination and violence against LGBT people must be addressed urgently as killings rise.

Where armed groups operate, the violence takes the form of announced campaigns. In Caquetá, armed groups ran "social cleansing" campaigns publicised through flyers targeting "drug addicts, prostitutes and faggots" and threatened a further wave; the Guardian's investigation of 30 July 2024 recorded that armed groups gave the trans woman Tatiana Cespedes one week to leave town or be killed, and trans women in that department reported few options beyond sex work. In Guajira, armed groups posted flyers from March 2024 carrying a kill list of named individuals under the wording "All will be military targets... homosexuals, lesbians, rapists, trans". The Guardian also quoted an activist stating that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, recording such killings as ordinary cases, and reported 41 trans women killed in Colombia in 2023 and eight between February and April 2024.

Targeted killings of trans people also occur in ordinary urban settings. Sara Millerey, a 32-year-old trans woman, was attacked in Bello, Antioquia, near Medellín in April 2025; a 28-second video of the assault circulated from 5 April showing her with fractured legs, arms and hands, flailing in a creek unable to swim, before she drowned. Her mother Sandra Borja stated, "They killed her for being who she was". President Petro ordered an urgent investigation and solidarity events were held in several cities. An international broadcaster reported on 6 August 2025 that anti-LGBTQ attacks were surging across the country, covering a wave of assaults through the Millerey case and attacks on same-sex couples.

Some of this violence has been prosecuted as an international crime rather than ordinary homicide. In July 2023 the Special Jurisdiction for Peace indicted 15 former rebels for war crimes and crimes against humanity against people of diverse sexual orientations and gender identities, with the state acknowledging that conflict-driven violence against these individuals constitutes gender persecution, a crime against humanity. The UN Human Rights Committee has registered concern over the same pattern, and a Colombian court has ruled on the treatment of a trans woman deprived of liberty, protecting the rights of trans detainees in the prison system.
tangentialFactors:
Colombia's framework is among the most developed in Latin America: the Constitutional Court made Colombia the fourth Latin American country to legalise same-sex marriage, and the notarial gender-marker route of 2015 removed the psychiatric and physical examinations that previously preceded a court order. Institutional reform of that scope sits alongside an enforcement record the UN Independent Expert described as disconnected from daily life.

The armed-group findings the sources carry come from Caquetá and Guajira, other departments, and are pattern indicators rather than evidence about Meta. Caquetá is where trans women were given one week to leave or be killed and where "social cleansing" flyers named trans women; Guajira is where a kill-list flyer named individuals for killing. The record also notes an armed-conflict displacement dynamic in Meta's own profile, which is why these comparators bear on the departmental assessment.

Two further tensions appear in the sources. Reporting indicates that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide as a category, so killings of trans women may be recorded as ordinary cases rather than as bias crimes. And the Attorney General's count of 35 LGBTI murders in five months of 2025 coexists with the government's reform programme that the UN expert praised.
localsOnly:
Trans Colombians change the sex marker on government-issued identification by signing a document before a notary, a route available since June 2015 and free of judicialordered bodily inspections or psychiatric assessments; Constitutional Court jurisprudence from 1993 recognises legal gender recognition on self-recognition without a surgical requirement. National identification documents have carried "trans" and "non-binary" markers since November 2025.

A national LGBTI policy requires public entities to recognise these rights in education, health care, prisons and as victims of armed conflict, and states that national entities may not refuse to recognise them. Same-sex marriage has been available since April 2016 and adoption by same-sex couples since 2015, and a 2011 law prohibits discrimination based on sexual orientation.

Residents deprived of liberty have judicial protection: a Colombian court ruled on the treatment of a trans woman in detention and on the rights of trans detainees in the prison system. A comprehensive trans law was still under legislative consideration in 2025, so the statutory layer beyond these court and policy provisions is not yet in force.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Meta-specific source appears in the inventory: the departmental entry yields no usable finding, and the national sources explicitly carry no Meta-specific legal, enforcement or incident data. Whether trans residents or visitors in Meta have encountered resistance at notaries, public entities or health services is unresolved and not sourced.

The record does not establish whether Meta's own departmental administration has implemented the 2015 notarial rule differently from other departments, nor whether any hate-crime or transfemicide prosecution has been brought in Meta. The classification question more broadly remains unresolved: the sources report an activist's statement that the prosecutor's office does not recognise transfemicide, but do not show whether that practice has since changed.

Whether the comprehensive trans law under legislative consideration in 2025 has since been enacted is not sourced here. The characterisation of a national "wave" of attacks on 6 August 2025 is the international broadcaster's framing of the reporting period and is not corroborated in the inventory by a separate count.
